title: Governance, risk, and compliance
summary: Decide what to do when a security requirement cannot be met.
body: ## Key use case

Set up a security exception process for teams that need to ship before they meet a requirement. Give them one place to request an exception and give leadership a clear record of who accepted the risk.
## Workflows

Have the requesting team explain the requirement, the exposure, and the temporary safeguard. Ask Security to assess the risk. Send the decision to the business owner, then assign a fix owner and expiry date. Schedule a review before expiry and require a fresh decision for any extension.
## Deliverables
Keep one exception register with the requirement, decision and approver, temporary safeguard, fix owner, deadline, and closure evidence. Start with the issue tracker your teams already use.
## Operating responsibilities
### What triggers it?
A team asks to miss a security requirement or a control check fails.
### Who owns the decision?
The business owner who can accept the risk, with Security advising on the exposure.
### Who performs the follow-up?
The engineer or team lead assigned to implement the fix.
### What verifies closure?
Check the permanent safeguard or record a newly approved, time-limited decision.
### What can leadership see when it breaks?
Open exceptions by risk, overdue fixes, and exceptions expiring soon.

title: Identity and access management
summary: Remove access when someone changes teams or leaves.
body: ## Key use case
Assign IT an access removal workflow for role changes and departures. Start with one application that has sensitive or privileged access, then expand to the other apps.
## Workflows

Use the employee roster to trigger a review. For a transfer, ask application owners which old permissions still serve a business need. For a departure, disable the central identity and check apps that have separate accounts. Assign each removal to an administrator and recheck the source application after the change.
## Deliverables
Maintain an app and owner inventory, a list of permissions reviewed, and one tracked task per removal. Record the account, permission, decision, due date, and verification result.
## Operating responsibilities
### What triggers it?
A person joins, changes role, or leaves, or an owner review is due.
### Who owns the decision?
The app or data owner decides whether access is needed. Established offboarding rules govern departing accounts.
### Who performs the follow-up?
IT or the application administrator changes the permission.
### What verifies closure?
Recheck the account and role in the source application after the change.
### What can leadership see when it breaks?
Orphaned accounts, privileged access awaiting review, and removals overdue by app.

title: Cloud and infrastructure security
summary: Protect a new cloud environment before it handles customer data.
body: ## Key use case
Set a minimum baseline for cloud accounts before they can handle production services or customer data. Assign a platform owner to apply it and an application owner to operate each account.
## Workflows

At account creation, record the owner and expected data. Enable central logs, restrict administrator access, and make sensitive storage private by default. Put those checks in the account creation template. Route failed checks to the account owner and require a documented decision for temporary exceptions.
## Deliverables
Keep an account inventory, the setup template and baseline checks, and a remediation queue. Attach the successful retest to each closed finding.
## Operating responsibilities
### What triggers it?
A new cloud account is requested or a scan detects a change from the baseline.
### Who owns the decision?
The infrastructure owner decides how to fix it. Security and the accountable business owner review exceptions.
### Who performs the follow-up?
The cloud platform team or service owner applies the change.
### What verifies closure?
Rerun the check and confirm the intended configuration directly in the cloud account.
### What can leadership see when it breaks?
Accounts without owners or logging, internet-facing findings, and high-risk drift past its deadline.

title: Application and product security
summary: Review a feature that lets customers export sensitive data.
body: ## Key use case
Require a lightweight security design review for features that expose sensitive data. Pilot it with a customer data export, where authorization, file delivery, and expiry can be checked directly.
## Workflows

Ask the feature engineer to draw the path from the export request to the download. Review who can request it, who can retrieve it, when the file expires, and what support can investigate. Translate decisions into tests and assign unresolved fixes before the release decision.
## Deliverables
Store the data flow sketch, design decisions, release conditions, and results in the feature ticket. Turn repeat decisions into reusable guidance for future export features.
## Operating responsibilities
### What triggers it?
A design introduces a sensitive operation or changes an existing access boundary.
### Who owns the decision?
The product and engineering owners decide whether to release, with Security reviewing unresolved risks.
### Who performs the follow-up?
The feature team changes the design and adds tests.
### What verifies closure?
Check that the agreed tests pass and confirm that required fixes are in the release.
### What can leadership see when it breaks?
High-risk reviews awaiting a decision, release conditions still open, and recurring design issues.

title: Software supply chain security
summary: Ship a release built from reviewed code and approved dependencies.
body: ## Key use case
Ask Engineering to show how a customer-facing release traces back to reviewed code and its dependencies. Start with the product that ships most frequently.
## Workflows

Require review for build configuration changes. Scope build credentials to the job and generate a component inventory for each release. When a dependency alert comes in, check whether the affected component is in production, assign the fix, and verify deployment of the updated release.
## Deliverables
Retain the component list, build provenance showing where the release came from, review approvals, and deployed version. Link each dependency fix to the affected and replacement releases.
## Operating responsibilities
### What triggers it?
A dependency or build configuration changes, a release is produced, or an alert applies to a shipped component.
### Who owns the decision?
The service owner decides the remediation. A designated release owner decides whether unresolved risk can ship under an approved exception.
### Who performs the follow-up?
The service or build platform team updates the package or pipeline.
### What verifies closure?
Confirm the deployed release contains the fixed component and can be traced to the approved build.
### What can leadership see when it breaks?
Unreviewed build changes, affected releases without owners, and dependency fixes past due.

title: Data security and privacy engineering
summary: Verify that a customer deletion request reaches downstream systems.
body: ## Key use case

Assign a privacy owner to run a test customer deletion through the product and its downstream systems. Use the result to find copies, delayed deletions, and unowned systems before a real request comes in.
## Workflows

Validate the requester and define the scope. Trace the customer identifier through databases, exports, analytics, and relevant vendors. Give each system owner a task. Ask Privacy and Legal to document justified retention or backup expiry and keep those items visible until resolved.
## Deliverables
Keep a data flow map, a system ownership list, the deletion ticket, and minimal completion evidence for each store. Keep raw customer data out of the evidence record.
## Operating responsibilities
### What triggers it?
A validated deletion request arrives or the retention period ends.
### Who owns the decision?
The privacy owner decides scope and any applicable retention exceptions with Legal when needed.
### Who performs the follow-up?
The owners of source and downstream systems perform the deletion.
### What verifies closure?
Check completion in each in-scope system and document any approved retention or backup expiry.
### What can leadership see when it breaks?
Requests nearing deadline, unverified downstream stores, and recurring exceptions by system.

title: Endpoint and workplace security
summary: Make sure laptops meet a baseline before accessing company apps.
body: ## Key use case
Set a device baseline for people accessing sensitive apps. Pilot it with company laptops and give IT a way to restore legitimate access when a check fails.
## Workflows

Enroll devices and verify encryption, updates, and endpoint protection. Test a sign-in when a device passes and when it fails. Publish instructions employees can follow to regain access. Pilot enforcement on one app before expanding, and require approvals and expiry for temporary exceptions.
## Deliverables
Keep the device inventory, baseline, coverage report, support instructions, and exception register. Record who owns the failed device check and whether it was fixed.
## Operating responsibilities
### What triggers it?
A device is enrolled, changes posture, or attempts to access an app with device requirements.
### Who owns the decision?
IT owns baseline enforcement. Security approves time-limited exceptions with the responsible business owner.
### Who performs the follow-up?
IT support and the employee bring the device back into compliance.
### What verifies closure?
Confirm device health in the management tool and confirm the user can sign in again.
### What can leadership see when it breaks?
Unmanaged devices, failed checks by reason, and exceptions or patches past due.

title: Vulnerability and exposure management
summary: Turn an internet-facing finding into a verified fix.
body: ## Key use case
Require verified closure for internet-facing vulnerabilities. Use a recent finding to test whether the team can identify the asset, reach the owner, and show the exposure is gone.
## Workflows

Confirm the affected asset, exposure, and business impact. Combine duplicate reports, assign a fix owner and deadline, and record any temporary safeguard. If the owner asks to defer, document the decision and a date to revisit it. Retest the deployed asset after the fix.
## Deliverables
Maintain a prioritized queue with the affected asset, owner, deadline, fix, exception if any, and retest evidence. Use an ownership queue for findings that arrive without a clear team.
## Operating responsibilities
### What triggers it?
A scan, external report, or new exposure identifies a potentially affected asset.
### Who owns the decision?
The service owner owns the fix. Security validates priority and reviews residual risk.
### Who performs the follow-up?
The team that operates the asset applies the remediation.
### What verifies closure?
Rerun the relevant check against the deployed asset and confirm the exposure is gone.
### What can leadership see when it breaks?
High-risk findings without owners, overdue internet-facing issues, and reopened findings.

title: Detection, response, and threat intelligence
summary: Respond to a suspicious sign-in from alert to recovery.
body: ## Key use case
Build one response workflow around suspicious sign-ins. Make sure a named responder can receive the alert, investigate it, and get help from someone who can contain the incident.
## Workflows

Collect identity logs, define the alert, and test that it reaches the on-call responder. Give the responder a checklist covering the user, active sessions, devices, and recent activity. Name the people who can contain the incident, approve communications, and authorize recovery. Exercise the handoffs in a tabletop.
## Deliverables
Keep the detection rule, response playbook, on-call contacts, timeline, recovery evidence, and corrective actions. Assign deadlines to gaps found in the exercise or incident.
## Operating responsibilities
### What triggers it?
An alert fires, a user reports suspicious activity, or a threat signal matches an exposed service.
### Who owns the decision?
The incident lead sets severity and response priorities, with Legal and Communications owning their decisions.
### Who performs the follow-up?
The on-call responder coordinates containment and the affected teams carry it out.
### What verifies closure?
Verify the account or service is safe to restore, then track corrective actions to completion.
### What can leadership see when it breaks?
Unacknowledged alerts, time to containment, repeat incident causes, and overdue corrective actions.

title: Third-party and supply chain risk
summary: Put a security review into the path of buying a vendor.
body: ## Key use case

Put vendor security intake inside the purchasing process. Ask Procurement to route trial and purchase requests through a short set of questions before an integration gets customer data or production access.
## Workflows

Ask what the vendor will receive, what it can connect to, and how critical it will be. Use the answers to decide review depth. Set limits and expiry for trials, and record approvals and contract conditions for sensitive vendors. Assign offboarding when the relationship ends.
## Deliverables
Maintain the vendor inventory, risk tier, approval record, contract conditions, and outstanding findings. Record proof of access removal and data disposition at exit.
## Operating responsibilities
### What triggers it?
A team requests a purchase or trial, a vendor’s access changes, or the contract ends.
### Who owns the decision?
The business owner accepts the business risk. Security and Legal advise or approve within their responsibilities.
### Who performs the follow-up?
Procurement coordinates, and IT or the app owner makes access changes.
### What verifies closure?
Confirm approval conditions are met, or verify the vendor’s access and data disposition at offboarding.
### What can leadership see when it breaks?
Vendors in use without approval, high-risk findings past due, and renewals arriving without reassessment.

title: AI security and governance
summary: Review an AI feature that can access customer data or take actions.
body: ## Key use case
Require a launch review for AI features that access customer data or can act on a user’s behalf. Start with a single product workflow and specify exactly what it may read, change, or send.
## Workflows

Document the intended use, permitted data sources, and tool permissions. Decide which actions require human review. Ask Engineering to test how the feature responds to untrusted instructions, attempts to access restricted data, and service failures. Name someone who can pause the feature if it behaves outside the approved scope.
## Deliverables
Keep the use-case record, permission boundaries, test cases and results, launch conditions, monitoring plan, and pause procedure.
## Operating responsibilities
### What triggers it?
A team proposes a new AI use case or changes its model, data access, or tool permissions.
### Who owns the decision?
The product owner owns launch, with Security, Privacy, and Legal reviewing risks they own.
### Who performs the follow-up?
The AI or product engineering team changes controls, tests behavior, and adds monitoring.
### What verifies closure?
Review the agreed tests against the deployed configuration and confirm launch conditions are met.
### What can leadership see when it breaks?
Unreviewed AI uses, failed evaluations, changes awaiting review, and incidents involving data or actions.

title: Security architecture and engineering
summary: Give teams a reusable way to handle application secrets.
body: ## Key use case
Give engineering teams a reusable way to manage service credentials. Ask the platform team to pilot the pattern with one service before requiring it broadly.
## Workflows

Choose a shared secrets store and define which service identity can retrieve each credential. Supply a working example, confirm access is logged, and test rotation without downtime. Review exceptions to learn where the default needs improvement.
## Deliverables
Maintain a reference design, a sample integration, an adoption list, and an exception register. Document how teams verify access restrictions, logging, and credential rotation.
## Operating responsibilities
### What triggers it?
A service needs a credential or a team discovers an existing credential managed outside the shared pattern.
### Who owns the decision?
The security architecture owner sets the default. The service owner owns adoption and exceptions.
### Who performs the follow-up?
The platform team builds the shared pattern, and service owners integrate it.
### What verifies closure?
Verify the service uses the shared store, can rotate the credential, and produces access logs.
### What can leadership see when it breaks?
Services outside the standard, expired exceptions, and repeated reasons teams cannot adopt the pattern.

title: Operational technology security
summary: Give a maintenance vendor timed access to equipment.
body: ## Key use case

Agree on a controlled maintenance process with the site operations lead. Start with one vendor visit and identify which equipment is in scope, when changes are safe, and who can restore normal operations.
## Workflows

Approve a named vendor identity, a maintenance window, and access limited to the equipment in scope. Have the site team record the change and check normal operation. At the end of the window, verify that temporary access is closed.
## Deliverables
Maintain the equipment inventory and owners, maintenance approval, session records where available, recovery steps, and access closure evidence.
## Operating responsibilities
### What triggers it?
A maintenance request requires outside access or a change to operational equipment.
### Who owns the decision?
The site operations owner approves the window and operational risk with Security advising on access.
### Who performs the follow-up?
The site technician coordinates the change, and the access administrator creates and removes vendor access.
### What verifies closure?
Verify that access expired and the site owner confirmed normal operation.
### What can leadership see when it breaks?
Standing vendor access, missed maintenance checks, and equipment changes without a recorded owner.

title: Hardware and firmware security
summary: Release a firmware update devices can verify and recover from.
body: ## Key use case
Require a verified firmware release process for one device family. Ask the release owner to demonstrate how devices confirm an update came from the company and recover if installation fails.
## Workflows

Identify the affected device models and versions. Require review before signing the release. Test installation and recovery on a small batch, agree on failure thresholds, and expand the rollout only after the pilot meets them.
## Deliverables
Keep the affected-device inventory, build and signing evidence, test results, rollout approval, and completion checks. Link the release to the defect or vulnerability it addresses.
## Operating responsibilities
### What triggers it?
A device defect or vulnerability requires an update, or a new version is ready to ship.
### Who owns the decision?
The hardware or firmware release owner approves rollout based on security and reliability checks.
### Who performs the follow-up?
Firmware engineers build the update, and device operations manages the rollout.
### What verifies closure?
Verify a sample of devices reports the expected version and that failure rates stay within the agreed limit.
### What can leadership see when it breaks?
Devices still on affected versions, rollout failures, and releases missing validation evidence.

title: Physical security
summary: Control and verify temporary access to an office or restricted room.
body: ## Key use case
Set a short approval and expiry process for temporary access to offices and restricted rooms. Start with contractor badges, where the sponsor, location, and end date can all be verified.
## Workflows

Require the host to name the visitor, purpose, permitted areas, and end time. Have Workplace issue time-limited access and apply escort requirements for sensitive areas. Verify expiry or badge return, and make it easy to report a lost badge.
## Deliverables
Keep the visitor record, sponsor, badge assignment and expiry, restricted-area approval, and any incident follow-up. Limit access to those logs to the teams with a business need.
## Operating responsibilities
### What triggers it?
A visit is requested, an employee leaves, or someone reports a lost badge.
### Who owns the decision?
The site or restricted-area owner approves access, with the host responsible for requesting it.
### Who performs the follow-up?
Workplace staff issue, collect, or revoke the badge.
### What verifies closure?
Check the access control system and confirm the badge can no longer open the relevant doors.
### What can leadership see when it breaks?
Overdue badges, access approvals without sponsors, and unusual events requiring follow-up.
